item.title: Shoppers helped pay Trump's tariffs. Refunds are boosting retailers' profits.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
American consumers helped foot the bill for President Donald Trump’s tariffs as retailers passed higher import costs on through price increases. Now the refunds are flowing back, and they are showing up in retailers’ profits rather than in shoppers’ bank accounts. Best Buy and Kohl’s both reported better-than-expected quarterly results on Tuesday, after Target beat expectations last week. Together, the three retailers recognized $387 million in tariff refund benefits in their latest quarters. The money traces back to February, when the Supreme Court ruled that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) did not authorize the president to impose tariffs, invalidating a significant portion of Trump’s tariff regime. As of Nov. 5, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) had certified approximately $128.4 billion in tariff refunds, including interest, and sent them to the Treasury Department for payment, according to a Nov. 10 filing with the U.S. Court of International Trade. Tariff refunds are boosting retailers’ profits Kohl’s reported third-quarter comparable sales growth of just 1.2%, yet its net income jumped to $254 million from $8 million a year earlier. Much of that came from one-time items: a $137 million tax benefit, a $61 million gain from the sale of two properties, and $45 million in tariff refund benefits, according to the company’s third-quarter earnings release . The department store chain has received approximately $190 million in tariff refunds this fiscal year. It now expects those refunds to add $1.03 to its full-year earnings per share, nearly a quarter of its raised forecast of $4.30 to $4.50. Best Buy reported comparable sales growth of 6.1%, its strongest in five years, in Jason Bonfig’s first earnings report as CEO . Net income more than doubled to $353 million from $140 million, according to the company’s earnings release . In May 2025, Best Buy’s then-CEO Corie Barry said the electronics retailer had already raised prices on some products to offset the costs of Trump’s tariffs. This quarter, the company recorded $41 million in tariff refund benefits, which helped lift profitability. Target has recognized approximately $1.3 billion in tariff refund benefits in the first nine months of its fiscal year, including $301 million in the third quarter alone. Its quarterly net income rose to $1.2 billion from $689 million, and tariff refunds accounted for $228 million of that after taxes, or nearly a fifth, according to Target’s third-quarter results . All three retailers are seeing sales rebound. But the refunds are boosting profits without requiring them to sell a single extra product. Shoppers paid a large share of the tariffs Best Buy was far from alone in passing higher import costs on to shoppers. An April analysis by Harvard Business School researchers , who tracked daily prices of nearly 360,000 products at five major U.S. retailers, estimated that consumers shouldered up to 43% of the tariff costs in the first seven months after the new tariffs were imposed. U.S. businesses absorbed the rest. Trump’s tariffs amounted to an average tax increase of $1,000 per U.S. household in 2025, according to estimates from the Tax Foundation . In February, Goldman Sachs economists estimated that tariffs had raised core PCE prices, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge, by about 0.7% through January. The effect outlasted the ruling. Researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and Columbia University estimated that consumer goods prices were still about 2% higher in August than they would have been without the tariffs imposed since early 2025. Some Americans who paid customs charges directly on overseas purchases are receiving refunds through shipping companies including FedEx , UPS , and DHL . The federal refund system offers no such relief to shoppers who paid higher prices at their local stores. Lawmakers are pressing companies to give the money back Earlier this month, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and fellow Democratic senators asked the Federal Trade Commission to investigate whether companies that raised prices in response to tariffs and then kept the refunds violated federal law. Warren’s office accused corporations of “pocketing tariff refunds after raising prices on consumers.” The senators cited responses from five major companies: Walmart , Nike , Apple , Target, and Energizer. None committed to directly reimbursing consumers who had paid higher prices because of the tariffs. Several major companies have either ruled out direct refunds to shoppers or remained silent on the issue, as Fortune previously reported . In August, Walmart said it was using its tariff refunds to lower prices, having received nearly all of the $2.9 billion it was owed. CBS News reported that the retailer cut prices on thousands of items in July. Target is doing the same. In August, Target CFO Jim Lee said the retailer would focus on lowering prices but made no commitment to directly refunding shoppers. The retailer said last week it had lowered prices on nearly 2,000 home, apparel, and accessories products during the third quarter, on top of more than 10,000 price reductions over the past year. But lowering prices for future purchases is different from compensating customers for past ones. A shopper who paid more for a television or a piece of furniture last year may have no reason to buy another one this holiday season, even if it is now cheaper. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com This article originally appeared on Fortune at https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/shoppers-helped-pay-trump-tariffs-083100398.html

item.title: Andrea Stewart-Cousins, 1st Black woman to lead N.Y. Senate, dies at 76
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
ALBANY, New York — Democratic state Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins, one of the highest-ranking Black women in New York state history, died Thursday evening, state officials announced Friday. “Throughout her decades in public service, Stewart-Cousins made a profound impact on the lives of New Yorkers,” New York Senate Democratic spokesperson Mike Murphy said. “She was a groundbreaking leader who shattered one of New York's highest glass ceilings, becoming the first woman to lead the New York State Senate.” Stewart-Cousins, 76, was reelected earlier this month to the top job in the Democratic-dominated chamber. She was preparing to preside over her party’s largest majority in modern history after Democrats captured at least 47 seats in the 63-member state Senate. It was too soon to determine Friday afternoon if Democrats will launch a race to succeed her or move forward with an interim leader. A Yonkers lawmaker, Stewart-Cousins was the first Black woman to lead what had been a notoriously fractious state Senate, which had long been ruled by Republicans. When Democrats came to power in 2019, Stewart-Cousins and state lawmakers passed a series of long-sought measures including criminal justice law changes and provisions like early voting. Known for wearing colorful scarfs, her friendly public demeanor obscured a hard-nosed tactician with a sarcastic streak. Behind the scenes she wouldn’t hesitate to discipline unruly rank-and-file members. Her death comes weeks before an Albany legislative session that’s expected to include debates over raising taxes and how to address voters’ sustained affordability concerns. “We’re going to be looking at the needs of New York, continuing to focus on affordability, the lives of working people, trying to figure out how to get the things people need,” Stewart-Cousins said in an interview with POLITICO earlier this month. Stewart-Cousins had been presiding over a Democratic conference in transition. Her longtime deputy, Mike Gianaris of Queens, retired in August, and she had batted away questions about her own retirement. Her ascension to Senate majority leader added the first woman to Albany’s fabled “three men in a room” — shorthand for the closed-door budget negotiations between the governor and legislative leaders. The role made Stewart-Cousins one of the most powerful elected officials in New York. She came out of the Westchester County Legislature. While serving there, she learned how to balance competing factions in a county whose demographics roughly mirror those of the state’s. It was there that she also developed her signature sartorial choice — always wearing a scarf, which she said she started doing because people confused her with the only other Black woman to win a seat at the county level. She first ran for Senate in 2004, losing by 18 votes. When she won two years later, she joined a tumultuous Democratic conference, with her first years in Albany marked by bitter feuds and power struggles. Her colleagues elevated her to minority leader in 2012 after her predecessor joined a long list of top senators facing indictments. Against all odds, she made it work. Democrats won 39 of the Senate’s 63 seats in 2018, giving members their first stable majority since World War II. And unlike every other modern instance when Senate Democrats won power, the conference under her leadership remained unified. It became the norm for socialists and moderates alike to begin their public statements with encomiums of “the tremendous leadership of our Andrea Stewart-Cousins.” “Most peoples’ experiences in the New York State Legislature involve a leader and a staff that would set the tone more than the members themselves,” Gianaris said in 2020 about her leadership style. “And Andrea takes a very different approach, where it’s the members that drive the decisions, and members that drive the agenda … It’s a much more bottom-up process than top-down.” The Senate long had a reputation as the place where progressive priorities met their demise in deep-blue New York. But it became arguably the center of left-leaning activism as soon as Stewart-Cousins became majority leader in 2019. The Legislature spent that year rapidly passing bottled-up legislation on subjects like immigration, tenant rights, and codifying abortion protections — a personal priority for her. Joe Anuta contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/27/trailblazing-ny-senate-majority-leader-dies-at-76-01184412

item.title: Lutnick in the hot seat as senators vow to crack down on AI chip leaks to China
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Senators in both parties say that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is in the hot seat in the wake of revelations that Nvidia sold billions of dollars’ worth of high-tech chips to a Singapore-based company whose former senior executive, Alice Huang, is accused of being a Chinese spy. Lawmakers in both parties criticized President Trump’s intervention to persuade Nvidia’s board to bring Jensen Huang back as its CEO after he admitted to the extramarital affair with Alice Huang, whom American intelligence said had contact with a Chinese spy agency. But while senators have limited ability to change Nvidia’s decision to rehire Jensen Huang, they can exert more pressure on Lutnick, whose department depends on appropriations from Congress. Black Friday-Cyber Monday Deals Black Friday deals are live: Apple, Dyson, Ninja and more Amazon's Black Friday sale is live with some of the lowest prices this year 40+ Black Friday deals at their lowest price this year BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission. “I think that Mr. Lutnick’s got a host of problems,” said Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.), the incoming chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee who also sits on the Senate Banking Committee, which will hear testimony from Huang next week. Warner suggested the Commerce Department may have allowed Nvidia to make sensitive technology sales to companies in addition to Megaspeed, the company connected to Alice Huang, that undermined restrictions on China’s access to advanced chips. “The idea that the Commerce Department has been allowing potentially not just some of these one-off descriptions of [chip sales] that Nvidia’s been doing but through other Chinese shell companies — we deserve answers,” he said. Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.), the current chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said he had warned the Trump administration that advanced chips were getting past export controls and called on Congress to pass legislation to tighten restrictions. “Congress has much to investigate and we will pass overwhelmingly bipartisan chip export-control bills, including my Chip Security Act, one way or the other,” Cotton posted on the social platform X. Lutnick is coming under heavy scrutiny from both Democrats and Republicans on Capitol Hill after media outlets reported that he resisted pressure from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio to put Megaspeed, the company previously affiliated with Alice Huang, on a trade blacklist. Bessent confronted Lutnick earlier this month over why the Commerce Department had not banned the sale of advanced AI chips to Megaspeed, according to The New York Times. Bessent told CNBC in an interview that he was frustrated over the delay in restricting chip sales and blamed the Commerce Department for not acting. “I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s,” he said, adding that the Commerce Department “has the pen” and suggesting that it should explain “their internal processes.” Democrats, who will control the Senate and House in January, are pressing for answers about whether Lutnick may have been motivated by a financial conflict of interest. They want to know whether data centers in Southeast Asian countries that supplied advanced computing power to China had financial ties to Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial services firm that Lutnick once led and is now run by his sons. Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), the incoming chair of the House Judiciary Committee, said Lutnick and other members of the Trump administration may “have converging personal, political, corporate and financial interests in making sure” Jensen Huang remains as Nvidia’s CEO. Lawmakers want to know what role Lutnick may have played in delaying the implementation of rules to restrict the sale of chips to companies such as Megaspeed and A201, a data center based in Malaysia, that allegedly provided China access to advanced computing power. The Commerce Department has said Lutnick has complied with all ethics rules. But key Republicans have joined Democrats in calling on Lutnick to testify about his role overseeing policies and regulations on chip exports. Senate Banking Committee Chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.) has asked Lutnick to appear before his panel next month to answer questions. Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) said the Commerce Department appeared to “knowingly” allow sensitive AI technology to skirt export restrictions. “It appears that they knowingly allowed this to happen. Scott Bessent has been saying, ‘Stop it.’ So I want to get both of them in front of a committee, put them under oath,” he said on NBC’s “Meet the Press.” “If Secretary Lutnick is giving our chips away, he needs to stop it, in my opinion,” he added. This has prompted speculation on Capitol Hill that Lutnick’s future leadership of the Commerce Department could be on shaky ground. Lutnick will have to answer tough questions about a new report in The Atlantic that he transferred federal agents who were tasked with investigating the smuggling of advanced AI chips to his personal security detail, taking those agents off a critical national security job. Incoming Senate Commerce Committee Chair Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) said she has “great concerns about his leadership of Commerce.” Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), a member of the Senate Banking Committee, said Lutnick should resign amid reports that the Commerce Department slow-walked export controls for AI chips. Tillis said Lutnick was briefed on the findings by U.S. intelligence agencies that Huang was having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy before Trump invited the Nvidia CEO to join him on Air Force One in Alaska en route to a trip to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing. He said Lutnick should have intervened to block Huang from joining the president, something that Rubio tried to do. “It was my understanding that Lutnick had been briefed on it too. Let’s just say for the sake of argument that the president was distracted and did not remember telling him about it. Lutnick should have damn well should have known,” Tillis said. He said it was not appropriate for Huang to join Trump on the high-level trip. He also cited what he called Lutnick’s “entanglements with investments in Nvidia.” Asked if Lutnick should resign, Tillis said: “I think he should roll.” The Hill reached out to the Commerce Department for comment. item.title: Two American Airlines planes clip wings before takeoff
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A piece of aircraft is seen on the ground after two jets clipped wings at Reagan National Airport [BBC] Two American Airlines jets hit each other at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport while taxiing for departure in Washington DC on Friday. One jet "clipped the wing" of the other at around 5:10 ET (22:10 GMT), the Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement. No injuries were reported, and the FAA plans to investigate. Both aircraft returned to the gate and were removed from service to be inspected by maintenance teams, American Airlines said. The incident happened at the same airport where 67 people died in a deadly collision between a jetliner and an Army helicopter in January 2025. "American Airlines Flight 638 clipped the wing of American Airlines Flight 2152 while taxiing for departure," the FAA said. Air traffic controllers can be heard on an audio recording saying two Boeing 737s clipped on the airport's runway. The controllers requested an emergency response and fire personnel to the plane, then directed the aircraft to return to the gate. The "wingtips of both Boeing 737-800s made contact", American Airlines said in a statement. The airline added that it is working to get affected passengers who were evacuated from both planes to their destinations as soon as possible. A passenger on flight 2152 headed to Chicago's O'Hare airport told the BBC that he felt a "large jolt" on the right side of the aircraft as they were taxiing before departure. The other plane, flight 638, was bound for Dallas-Fort Worth airport. The passenger added that the "aircraft shook quite violently" upon impact and he heard gasps inside the cabin. He described the moment as "tense", but that nobody seemed to be hurt. As the passenger looked out the window he saw what appeared to be the tip of the aircraft wing [BBC] As he looked out the window, he saw a piece of the aircraft on the ground. It looked like the "tip of the wing", he said, describing how the other aircraft's wing was overlapping his plane's wing. The BBC has contacted American Airlines about reports of the broken wingtip. As they taxied back to the gate, the passenger said he saw a truck pick up the piece that had fallen. The fact that this isn't the first incident at this airport was "definitely scary", the passenger said. Last year, there was a deadly mid-air collision between another American Airlines flight and a military helicopter at Reagan National. The 64 people on the passenger plane and three US Army members on the Black Hawk helicopter all died in the crash. The aircraft, en route to land at the DC airport after leaving from Wichita, Kansas, was sent careening into the Potomac River upon impact with the military helicopter. It was later determined that the helicopter was receiving faulty altitude data, causing it to fly higher than intended. Reagan National Airport is the smaller of the two DC-area airports and caters mostly to domestic flights. It sits right near the sprawl of the US capital, the White House and the Pentagon. Earlier this week, the US Army said it planned to resume helicopter test flights near Reagan airport, according to CBS News, BBC's US News partner. The flights were paused following last year's incident. BBC has contacted the Pentagon for comment. NEW YORK — New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani successfully underwent surgery to repair his Achilles tendon on Friday, his spokesman said. The mayor is expected to make a full recovery and is now "resting comfortably at Gracie Mansion" after the roughly hour-long procedure , Mamdani's press secretary, Joe Calvello. Mamdani won't be in attendance at the rescheduled Thanksgiving Day parade , now taking place on Saturday, as a result of the surgery. "It's one thing I'm very disappointed about. I've been looking forward to attending this parade," Mamdani said during a security briefing Wednesday night. "I will not be able to make it because of the doctor's orders." First Deputy Mayor Dean Fuleihan is running day-to-day operations, per the City Charter. Mamdani tore the tendon while playing a friendly game of soccer with the City Hall news corps last week. During that game, he burst onto the field going full-force and without warming up — and then collapsed on the field with just a few minutes left in the game. He's expected to be in a boot for six to eight weeks, and won't play soccer or other sports for another nine months. The mayor called himself "the first mayor to ever have to go on a multi-month biking hiatus because he tore his Achilles in a fit of 35-year-old non-stretching hubris." Other mayors have also undergone surgery while in office, including Mayor Bill de Blasio, who went under the knife for meniscus surgery and a hernia in 2015. item.title: More Trump officials are turning to military housing as some cite security concerns
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Military housing in Washington has traditionally been home to generals and other senior officers. Now, some of President Donald Trump ’s top civilian officials are moving in, too. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC he is living on a U.S. military base after receiving unspecified threats from Iran earlier this month. “If the Iranians are after me, it means that they are being squeezed. We’re going to continue squeezing them,” Bessent said Nov. 20. He’s not alone. Several current and former Trump officials have lived on military installations, with threats, harassment or other security concerns factoring into some of the moves. Here’s who has lived in military housing, why and what the arrangements cost. More: Treasury's Bessent moved to military base after Iranian threats Who else lives on a military base? Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on a podcast earlier this year that he and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth are neighbors. Both live at Fort Lesley J. McNair , an Army installation in Washington, D.C., according to The Washington Post. White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and his family moved into military housing in 2025 after leaving their Virginia home. The White House said the family faced an “elaborate, well-documented stalking, doxing, and threat campaign” targeting their residence. Attorney General Todd Blanche also was recently relocated to a military base over safety concerns, CNN reported . Former Attorney General Pam Bondi lived on a military base last year, according to CNN. Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem lived at Joint Base Anacostia-Bolling toward the end of her tenure, USA TODAY Network member Nashville Tennessean previously reported . Why are Trump officials living on military bases? Security concerns have factored into several of the moves. Bessent has cited threats from Iran, while the White House said threats and harassment prompted the Miller family’s relocation. The Atlantic previously reported that Miller moved into military housing in 2025 after facing harassment at his Virginia home. Military installations offer controlled access and existing base security. But civilian officials’ use of military housing has also raised questions about housing traditionally designated for senior military personnel. What do officials pay for military housing? Civilian officials are required to pay rent for military housing, though rates vary by residence and the rules governing the arrangement. The arrangements have drawn congressional scrutiny. The Army was preparing to spend $137,297 on repairs and upgrades to Pete Hegseth ’s Fort McNair residence, CNN reported. The Pentagon must report to the House Armed Services Committee on political appointees living in military housing, including the legal authority for the arrangements and rental costs. Rep. George Whitesides, D-Calif., who pushed for the oversight, has also raised questions about whether political appointees are paying fair-market rates. Have Cabinet officials lived on military bases before? Yes, but the practice has historically been unusual. Robert Gates became the first defense secretary to live in military housing while serving under Presidents George W. Bush and Barack Obama. The Pentagon argued in 2008 that using existing base security could save taxpayers money compared with providing around-the-clock security at a private residence. Jim Mattis, Trump’s first-term defense secretary and Mike Pompeo, first-term secretary of state, later lived in military housing, according to The New York Times .
